analysis.one_liner: Caps the consumer protection bureau's unspent funds at 5% of its budget and sends the excess to the Treasury.
analysis.headline: The bill to cap the consumer bureau's unspent funding balance was introduced in May 2025 with 6 Republican cosponsors and referred to committee, where it has sat without a hearing or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) is funded directly by the Federal Reserve rather than by annual congressional appropriations. This bill would limit how much money the bureau can hold unspent in reserve to 5% of its annual funding, and would require it to transfer any excess to the Treasury's general fund. It would also require the bureau to describe its use of unspent balances in an annual report. Supporters frame this as budget discipline over an agency that operates outside the normal congressional spending process; critics see it as a way to siphon resources from the agency that polices banks, lenders, and debt collectors.
analysis.who_benefits: Banks, credit card issuers, debt collectors, and other financial companies regulated by the CFPB benefit if the bill passes, because a hard cap on the bureau's unspent reserves limits the cushion it can use to fund enforcement, rulemaking, and consumer refunds without going back for more money. Critics of the CFPB also benefit in that the bill adds a reporting requirement and a fiscal check on an agency funded outside the normal appropriations process.

how_it_helps.text: It caps the consumer bureau's unspent funding balance at 5% of its annual funding level and requires any excess to be transferred to the Treasury's general fund.
It requires the bureau's annual financial report to describe how it uses unspent balances, adding a layer of public accounting.

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary consumers who rely on the CFPB to police mortgage servicing, credit card fees, credit reports, and debt collection would bear any cost, in the form of a slightly smaller, less flexible enforcement agency; taxpayers gain only trivially from the sweep of small excess balances to the Treasury.

drawbacks.text: Forcing the CFPB to surrender unspent funds to the Treasury rather than carry them forward could leave the agency short when it needs money for a surge in enforcement or consumer redress, since its funding does not come from annual appropriations.

The cap applies to a regulator of banks and lenders, so any constraint on its resources tends to slow the enforcement and refund work that recovers money for consumers; the bill includes no offsetting strengthening of that mission.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's stated goal — a modest, transparent reserve cap — is reasonable on its face, and returning a small excess to the Treasury saves taxpayers a little. But because the CFPB is one of the few regulators whose funding the industry cannot lobby over through the appropriations process, even a small funding constraint carries outsized weight for an agency whose entire mission is policing that same industry. The cost to consumers of slightly slowed enforcement is hard to quantify, and the bill's practical effect in a Congress where it has not moved is likely nil.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Financial Services Committee, which has taken no action on it; no committee vote or floor vote has occurred.

narrative.text: Rep. Troy Downing introduced the CFPB Budget Integrity Act on May 1, 2025, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
The bill's only action since referral is that referral; the committee has not held a markup or sent it to the floor.
Six House Republicans cosponsored the bill; no Democrats have.
The bill would amend the Consumer Financial Protection Act to cap the CFPB's unobligated balances at 5% of its annual funding, with excess transferred to the Treasury general fund.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nothing has happened yet, so no one has gained or lost; banks and lenders are better off to the extent the bill sits idle rather than actually passing, while consumers keep the bureau at full current strength.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one yet; the bill sits idle

sides.party_line_note: All seven sponsors and cosponsors are Republicans, and the bill sits in a committee controlled by the same party, so the dividing line is less between parties than between a small group of critics of the CFPB and the broader chamber that has not acted.

industries.industry: Banks, lenders, and other companies regulated by the CFPB
industries.note: The CFPB writes and enforces rules on mortgages, credit cards, debt collection, and fees, and has returned billions to consumers; any mechanism that trims its funding cushion makes it a slightly weaker cop on the beat for the firms it polices.
Excess unspent balances would be swept into the general fund rather than carried by the bureau, a small fiscal benefit spread across all taxpayers.

analysis.trajectory: Bills referred to the House Financial Services Committee without early scheduling routinely die there, and this one has no hearing or markup four months after introduction; unless the committee acts, it will likely expire at the end of the 119th Congress without a vote.
